doc.title: Delfeayo Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Birth in New Orleans, segregated hospitals and integrated schooling
summary: Marsalis gives his birth date and hospital, notes segregation in the 1960s, and describes his parents choosing integrated school, which was easier for him than for Branford and Wynton.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Delfeayo Ferdinand Marsalis. You got to get the order right. July 28, 1965. What else?
I was born in New Orleans.
Do you remember which hospital? Or, do you know which hospital?
Flint Goodridge. In fact then there was only one or two options, I believe.
For folks of color. It would have been . . .
Oh yeah. It would have been . . .
So what you are saying is, there was still segregation.
Maybe that’s not known. That’s not the official record for our country.

Oh, come on. Anybody that lived in the South knows that. I think that it was the difference between Branford and Wynton. They were the first generation that was not –where it wasn’t forced busing. They had the choice to go to an integrated school. My parents made that choice for us, so that we would have to deal with integration early on. So we were fairly much prepared for whatever came after that. Branford and Wynton had it a little tougher than me. Even that five year difference, it made a difference in terms of how the students reacted.
How did they react to you?

It was, I guess, less contempt. I think – Wynton would tell a story. They gave him a stuffed monkey for Christmas. Like when it came time, you’d have to exchange presents. But for me it wasn’t as obvious. The kids were pretty cool.

No, no problems from the teachers. At that point, I think everyone realized that we had to move in a forward direction. I was at that point a very good student. I was always – I was never absent, and I had straight A’s at that point. So teachers were cool with me. Taking care of business.
